How a print is made Press Next and watch a print being made. Press Next and watch a print being made. A print is a mark you make by pressing. You put paint on something, press it on the paper, and lift it off. The paint goes on the stamp. The stamp presses on the paper. You lift it, and the mark is left behind. Press again, and you get the same mark again. Children rub the stamp round and round. Press it straight down, then lift it straight up. Press Next and watch.

Things that print Lots of things can make a print. Tap each one to hear what it prints. Lots of things can make a print. Tap each one to hear what it prints. You can print with almost anything that has a shape or a bumpy side. Every thing prints its own marks. A leaf prints its lines. A sponge prints tiny dots. Bubble wrap prints rows of round dots. A bottle top prints a circle. Half a potato prints the shape you cut into it. Your hand prints your hand. Children think only a stamp from a shop can print. Look around. Leaves, sponges and bottle tops all print. Tap all six and listen.

What will it print? Think about the bumpy side of each thing. Will it print lines, dots or a shape? Think about the bumpy side of each thing. Will it print lines, dots or a shape? Before you print, you can guess what the print will look like. Look at the side that will touch the paper. A fork has lines, so it prints lines. Bubble wrap has bumps, so it prints dots. A bottle top has a round rim, so it prints a circle shape. Children look at the colour of the thing. The colour does not matter. The bumpy side does. Look at the bumpy side, then tap the bin.

Pick the printer Each picture needs a different print. Which thing would print it? Tap one. Each picture needs a different print. Which thing would print it? Tap one. Artists choose the tool that makes the mark they need. Grass wants lines, so pick something that prints lines. A ladybird's spots want dots. A row of stars wants a star shape. Children pick the thing they like best. Pick the one that prints what the picture needs. Read what the picture needs, then tap.

Print a pattern Each row is printed with stamps. Tap the print that comes next. Then print your own pattern. Each row is printed with stamps. Tap the print that comes next. Then print your own pattern. A printed pattern repeats, just like a pattern of tiles. This time some patterns have three or four prints before they start again. Say the prints out loud. Listen for where the pattern starts again. Then tap what comes next. At the end, print your own. It only counts if it repeats! Children stop listening after two prints. Some patterns are longer. Keep going until it starts again. Say it out loud, then tap.

A cloth printed with stamps This cloth was printed with stamps, in the manner of the adinkra cloths printed in Ghana. Tap the things in it. This cloth was printed with stamps, in the manner of the adinkra cloths printed in Ghana. Tap the things in it. In Ghana, people print adinkra cloth with stamps carved from a calabash, a hard fruit shell. The stamps are pressed in rows, again and again. Tap the circle stamps. Tap the lines between the squares. They were drawn with a comb. Tap the diamond stamps and the flower stamps. Children think every shape was drawn one at a time. Look how the same shape comes again. That is a stamp. Tap three things and listen.

Print spotter Which one is it? Tap the answer. Which one is it? Tap the answer. Every question here is about printing. You have met every one of them. Think about paint, press and lift, and what each thing prints. Read it, look at the picture, then tap.

Artists change things to make them even better. Tap the thing you made first.

Colours have feelings Colours can make us feel things. Tap each set of colours to hear how it feels. Colours can make us feel things. Tap each set of colours to hear how it feels. Colours do more than show what a thing is. They can make a picture feel happy, calm, sleepy or stormy. Warm colours feel sunny and happy. Cool colours feel calm and fresh. Pale colours feel soft and gentle. Dark colours feel quiet or stormy. Bright colours feel busy and excited. Children think there is one right feeling for each colour. Colours can feel different to different people. Say how it feels to YOU. Tap all six and listen.

Tints and shades White makes a colour lighter. Black makes it darker. Guess what each mix makes, then tap the two pots. White makes a colour lighter. Black makes it darker. Guess what each mix makes, then tap the two pots. A colour with white added is called a tint. It is lighter. A colour with black added is called a shade. It is darker. Purple and white make light purple, a tint. Green and black make dark green, a shade. Always add just a little black. A little black goes a long way. Children pour in lots of black and the colour disappears. A tiny bit of black is enough. Tap your guess, then tap the two pots.

Red, from light to dark Here is red with more and more white or black in it. Put the reds in order, from lightest to darkest. Here is red with more and more white or black in it. Put the reds in order, from lightest to darkest. One colour can be light or dark. Adding white makes it lighter. Adding black makes it darker. Find the palest red first. Then the next one. End with the darkest. Children put bright red first. Look at how PALE each one is. Tap the lightest one first.

How does it feel? Here are some pictures, told in words. Which feeling do their colours USUALLY give: happy, calm or stormy? Tap the bin. Here are some pictures, told in words. Which feeling do their colours USUALLY give: happy, calm or stormy? Tap the bin. One way to look at a lot of pictures is to group them by how they feel. Artists and galleries do this too. Warm, bright colours often feel happy. Pale and cool colours often feel calm. Dark colours and sharp shapes often feel stormy. Children sort by what is IN the picture. Sort by how the COLOURS make you feel. Read it, feel it, then tap the bin.

Colours for a feeling You want your picture to feel a certain way. Which colours would do it? Tap them. You want your picture to feel a certain way. Which colours would do it? Tap them. When you know how you want a picture to feel, you can choose its colours on purpose. A hot day wants warm colours. A quiet lake wants cool colours. A soft blanket wants pale tints. A forest at night wants dark shades. Children use every colour in the box. Choose the colours that give the feeling. Read the picture, then tap the colours.

Two paintings, two feelings Two paintings feel very different. Is each thing in BOTH of them, or only in one? Two paintings feel very different. Is each thing in BOTH of them, or only in one? Artists compare paintings and say what is the same and what is different. Then they say which feeling each one gives. Both paintings have a sky. Only one has a sun. Only one is mostly dark colours. Children say 'one is day and one is night' and stop. Look for the colours too. Look at both paintings, then tap a bin.

Over and under Press Next and watch how a weave is made. Press Next and watch how a weave is made. Weaving is going over and under, again and again. It turns loose threads into something strong. The threads stretched on the loom are the warp. The thread you weave in is the weft. The weft goes over one warp thread and under the next. The next row goes the other way. Children go over two threads at once. Over ONE, under ONE. Press Next and watch.

Things people weave People weave all over the world, and even some birds weave. Tap each one to hear about it. People weave all over the world, and even some birds weave. Tap each one to hear about it. Weaving is one of the oldest ways of making things. People weave cloth, baskets, mats, hats and chair seats. A basket is woven from grass or reed. A scarf is woven from wool. Some birds weave their nests from grass. A straw hat is woven from dry grass. Children think weaving is only for cloth. Anything made by going over and under is weaving. Tap all six and listen.

steps.h: Make a paper weave, in order
steps.t: Make a paper weave, in order A paper weave is made in steps. Tap them in the order you would do them. A paper weave is made in steps. Tap them in the order you would do them. You can weave with paper. A sheet with slits is the warp, and strips of paper are the weft. First cut slits in a folded sheet, and cut some strips, with a grown-up. Weave the first strip over, under. Weave the next strip under, over. Push them close, and glue the ends. Children weave every strip the same way. The next strip starts the OTHER way. Tap what you do first.

What to weave with Each weaving needs a different material. Which would work? Tap one. Each weaving needs a different material. Which would work? Tap one. The material decides what the weaving is like. Wool makes it soft. Ribbon makes it shiny. Sticks make it strong. A warm scarf wants something soft. A party mat wants something shiny. A strong frame wants something stiff. A mat for the rain wants something that stays dry. Children pick the prettiest one. Pick the one that does the JOB. Read what it is for, then tap.

Fix the weave These weaves have a problem. Why did it go wrong? Which change fixes it? Tap one and see. These weaves have a problem. Why did it go wrong? Which change fixes it? Tap one and see. When a weave goes wrong, ask why. Then change the one thing that fixes it. Gaps between the strips: push them close. A strip that falls out went on top, not over and under. Strips sliding out at the edge: glue the ends. Children pull it all out and start again. Find the ONE thing that went wrong. Tap a change and see what it does.

A weaving on a loom This weaving is still on its loom. Tap the parts to find out what the weaver did. This weaving is still on its loom. Tap the parts to find out what the weaver did. A loom holds the warp threads tight while you weave. People weave on looms all over the world. Tap the warp: the threads at the top, still waiting. Tap the weft: the colours going over and under. Tap the stripes, and the loom itself. Children call every thread a string. Weavers say warp and weft. Tap three things and listen.

steps.h: Flat, or all the way round?
steps.t: Flat, or all the way round? A painting is flat. A sculpture you can walk all the way round. Tap each one to hear about it. A painting is flat. A sculpture you can walk all the way round. Tap each one to hear about it. A painting has one side. You look at it from the front. A sculpture has a front, a back and sides. You can walk round it. A clay pot is a sculpture you can hold. A statue is a sculpture in a park or a square. A snowman and a sandcastle are sculptures too. Children think a sculpture must be big and made of stone. Anything you make in the round is a sculpture. Tap all six and listen.

Score and slip Press Next and watch how potters join two pieces of clay so they stay joined. Press Next and watch how potters join two pieces of clay so they stay joined. In Grade 1 you pressed wet clay onto wet clay. That join can fall apart when it dries, so potters use score and slip to join clay for good. Scratch both pieces with a fork. That is scoring. Dab on slip: clay mixed with water until it is runny. Press them together and smooth the join. Children just squash the pieces together. Scratch, slip, press, smooth. Every time. Press Next and watch.

Will it join? Will each pair join and stay joined? Think about why, then tap the bin. Will each pair join and stay joined? Think about why, then tap the bin. When two things will not join, an artist asks why. Is it too dry? Too smooth? Is there nothing to hold them? Scored clay with slip joins. Dry clay will not stick to wet clay. Two smooth pebbles have nothing to hold them. Children guess. Ask WHY it would or would not join. Think why, then tap the bin.

Make it stand up These sculptures have a problem. Why did it happen? Which change fixes it? Tap one and see. These sculptures have a problem. Why did it happen? Which change fixes it? Tap one and see. A sculpture has to stand up in the real world. When it falls, look for why. A leg that falls off was not scored and slipped. A tower that tips over needs a wider bottom. A head that droops needs a thicker neck. Children add more clay everywhere. Fix the ONE thing that is wrong. Tap a change and see what it does.

What to build it from Each sculpture needs a different material. Which one would work? Tap one. Each sculpture needs a different material. Which one would work? Tap one. Every material does something different. Clay squashes and holds a shape. Boxes are light. Pipe cleaners bend. A tall, light tower wants boxes. A snake to hang up wants something bendy and light. A shiny robot wants foil. A heavy bottom wants stones. Children use clay for everything. Choose the material that does the job. Read what it is for, then tap.

steps.h: A clay head from long ago
steps.t: A clay head from long ago This clay head is drawn in the manner of heads made in Nigeria more than two thousand years ago. Tap the parts. This clay head is drawn in the manner of heads made in Nigeria more than two thousand years ago. Tap the parts. Long ago, in what is now Nigeria, people made heads from clay and fired them hard. Artists of the Nok culture made some of the oldest clay figures in West Africa. Tap the eyes. They were cut into the wet clay. Tap the hair. It was pressed in rows. Tap the mouth and the ears. Children think the eyes were painted on. Look closely. They were cut and pierced. Tap three things and listen.

Treasures from a nature walk Artists go outside to look and collect. Tap each treasure to hear about it. Artists go outside to look and collect. Tap each treasure to hear about it. A park, a garden or a path is full of shapes, colours and textures. Artists collect small things to look at closely and remember the walk. A leaf has lines and a jagged edge. A feather is soft, with thin lines. A pebble is round and smooth. Some artists make art right there, outside, from what they find. Children pick flowers that are still growing. Only collect things that have already fallen. Never put anything you find in your mouth, and wash your hands when you get home. Tap all six and listen.

Treasures by touch Imagine touching each treasure. Is it rough, smooth or soft? Tap the bin. Imagine touching each treasure. Is it rough, smooth or soft? Tap the bin. Sorting your treasures by how they feel is a way of recording the walk. Bark is rough and scratchy. A pebble is smooth. A feather is soft. Children sort by colour instead. Think about how it FEELS under your fingers. Imagine touching it, then tap the bin.

Autumn leaves, light to dark These leaves fell in autumn. Put them in order, from the lightest to the darkest. These leaves fell in autumn. Put them in order, from the lightest to the darkest. In places with an autumn, leaves change colour before they fall. Some are pale, some are bright, some are dark. Find the palest leaf first. Then the next one. End with the darkest brown. Children put red first because it is bright. Bright is not the same as light. Look at how PALE it is. Tap the lightest one first.

A leaf, looked at closely Artists look very closely before they draw. Tap the parts of this leaf. Artists look very closely before they draw. Tap the parts of this leaf. When you look closely, a plain leaf is full of lines and shapes. Tap the middle vein. Tap the little veins. Tap the jagged edge, and the stalk. Children see 'a leaf' and stop looking. Look for the lines inside it. Tap three things and listen.

Draw the lines you found Look at each treasure and draw the line it has. The card tells you which tool to use. Look at each treasure and draw the line it has. The card tells you which tool to use. You have just looked closely at a leaf. Now draw the lines you found. At home, you can draw a real leaf from life. The middle of a leaf has a straight line: its vein. The edge of a leaf is jagged, like a zigzag. A pebble is round. Draw all the way round and back to the start. A ladybird has dots. Children draw a leaf they imagine. Think of the leaf you looked at. Then draw. Look, then draw.

Then: pick one, and say what you would change next time. There is no wrong answer to that. Children think changing something means it was bad. It was not bad. Artists change things to make them even better. Tap the thing you made first.

Tear, cut and stick Press Next and watch a collage being made. Press Next and watch a collage being made. A collage is a picture made by sticking pieces on. The pieces can be paper, cloth, foil, anything flat. Tearing makes a soft, furry edge. Cutting makes a sharp, clean edge. Pieces can overlap: one on top of another. A little glue is enough. Children cover the paper in glue first. Put a little glue on each piece, not on the whole paper. Press Next and watch.

Collage materials Almost anything flat can go in a collage. Tap each one to hear what it adds. Almost anything flat can go in a collage. Tap each one to hear what it adds. Every material adds something different to a collage. Tissue paper is thin enough to see through. Magazine pages are full of colours. Fabric is soft. Foil is shiny. Wool makes fluffy lines. Card is stiff. Children only use plain paper. Try the shiny, the soft and the see-through ones too. Tap all six and listen.

Pick by colour You are making a collage. Which piece has the right colour for each part? Tap it. You are making a collage. Which piece has the right colour for each part? Tap it. In a collage, you can find a colour instead of painting it. You choose each piece because of its colour. An apple wants a red piece. A leaf wants a green piece. The sea wants blue. Children pick the piece they like and colour over it. Find a piece that is already the right colour. Read the part, then tap the piece.

Tear it or cut it? Some things have soft edges and some have sharp ones. Would you tear it or cut it? Tap the bin. Some things have soft edges and some have sharp ones. Would you tear it or cut it? Tap the bin. Tearing and cutting give different edges. Choose the one that looks like the real thing. A cloud has a soft edge, so tear it. A roof has straight, sharp edges, so cut it. Children cut everything. Look at the edge of the real thing first. Think about the edge, then tap the bin.

Show how it feels These collages do not quite show what their maker meant. What could you add? Tap one and see. These collages do not quite show what their maker meant. What could you add? Tap one and see. When a picture does not say what you mean, add something that shows it. Artists often stick collage onto a painting to show how things feel. A flat trunk: add rough, torn paper for bark. A plain sea: add layers of blue and green tissue. A dull night sky: add shiny foil stars. Children start again. Add ONE thing that shows it. Tap a change and see what it does.

steps.h: A paper cut, folded and cut
steps.t: A paper cut, folded and cut This red paper cut is drawn in the manner of Chinese paper cutting. Tap the parts to find out how it was made. This red paper cut is drawn in the manner of Chinese paper cutting. Tap the parts to find out how it was made. In China, people have cut pictures from paper for more than a thousand years. They fold the paper first, then cut. Tap the fold line down the middle. Tap the holes that were cut out. Tap the other half. Is it the same? Children think both halves were cut one at a time. The paper was folded, so one cut makes both halves. Tap three things and listen.

steps.h: Art tools that are not brushes
steps.t: Art tools that are not brushes Artists use cameras, tablets and even their own bodies. Tap each one to hear what it does. Artists use cameras, tablets and even their own bodies. Tap each one to hear what it does. Not every art tool leaves paint on paper. Some tools help you see, keep or record. A camera keeps a picture of something. A drawing app lets you draw and change it again. A magnifying glass shows tiny details. A torch makes shadows. Your body can dance a line. Children think art on a screen is not real art. A photo or a drawing on a tablet is art too. Tap all six and listen.

Which tool for the job? Each job needs a different tool. Which one would you use? Tap it. Each job needs a different tool. Which one would you use? Tap it. Choosing the right tool is part of being an artist. To keep a picture of something, use a camera. To see tiny lines, use a magnifying glass. To draw and change it, use a drawing app. To catch a sound, use a sound recorder. Children use the tablet for everything. Pick the one that does the job best. Read the job, then tap the tool.

steps.h: Take a good photo, in order
steps.t: Take a good photo, in order Taking a good photo has steps. Tap them in the order you would do them. Taking a good photo has steps. Tap them in the order you would do them. A good photo does not happen by luck. Photographers do the same steps every time. First choose what to take. Then move close or step back until it fills the screen. Hold very still and press the button. Look at the photo. If it is blurry, take another. Children press the button while they are still moving. Hold still first. Then press. Tap what you do first.

Close-up or far away? Each photo was taken close up or far away. Which is it? Tap the bin. Each photo was taken close up or far away. Which is it? Tap the bin. A close-up shows one small thing, very big. A far-away photo shows a lot of things, small. The spots on one ladybird filling the photo: close-up. A whole mountain: far away. Children think far away means blurry. Far away means you can see the whole big thing. Think about how much you can see, then tap the bin.

Draw how you moved Stand up and move, then draw the line your body made. The card tells you which tool to use. Stand up and move, then draw the line your body made. The card tells you which tool to use. When you move, your body draws lines in the air. Artists record a movement as a mark. Hopping forward makes a zigzag. Spinning round makes a circle. Swaying gently makes a wavy line. Stamping makes dots. Stretching up tall makes a straight line. Children draw the person, not the movement. Draw the LINE the movement made. Move first, then draw.

A flip book Press Next and watch how a flip book makes a picture move. Press Next and watch how a flip book makes a picture move. A cartoon is lots of pictures, each a tiny bit different, shown very fast. That is called animation. Draw a ball at the top of the first page. On the next page, draw it a little lower. Keep going, a little lower each time. Flip the pages fast, and the ball bounces. Children change the picture a lot on each page. Change it just a little. Then it moves smoothly. Press Next and watch.

steps.h: What goes in an art corner?
steps.t: What goes in an art corner? An art corner is a place to look at art and get ideas. Tap each thing to hear why it belongs. An art corner is a place to look at art and get ideas. Tap each thing to hear why it belongs. An art corner is a small gallery in your classroom or at home. It holds art from everywhere, and your own work too. Art from far away shows how other people make things. Art from long ago shows how people made things before us. Your own work shows how far you have come. Children think only 'best' work goes in. Every kind of work belongs. It is for looking and learning. Tap all six and listen.

Group the art corner One way to hang an art corner is by how each thing was made. Printed, woven, clay or collage? Tap the bin. One way to hang an art corner is by how each thing was made. Printed, woven, clay or collage? Tap the bin. A gallery groups its art so people can see how things connect. You can group by colour, by feeling, or by how it was made. A leaf print was printed. A paper weave was woven. A pinch pot is clay. A tissue-paper sea is a collage. Children group by what the picture shows. Group by HOW it was made. Think how it was made, then tap the bin.

Two artists, one idea A cloth printer and a tile maker both made patterns. Is each thing in BOTH works, or only in one? A cloth printer and a tile maker both made patterns. Is each thing in BOTH works, or only in one? Artists connect works that are far apart. A cloth from Ghana and a tiled wall can share an idea. Both have a pattern that repeats. Both put their shapes in squares. Only one has stars. Only one has circles. Children only see the differences. Look for the idea they SHARE. Look at both, then tap a bin.

Kind words for every artist These works are in your art corner. Say something kind and true about what is really in each one. These works are in your art corner. Say something kind and true about what is really in each one. Every artist deserves a kind word, near or far, old or new. The best kind word names something that is really there. The weaver made stripes. 'I love your stripes' is about the weaving. 'Your clay hair is neat' is about a different work. Children praise what they wish was there. Look first. Then name what IS there. Look, then tap the comment that is about it.

Get the corner ready Before the art corner opens, three things need fixing. Work out why, then tap the change that fixes it. Before the art corner opens, three things need fixing. Work out why, then tap the change that fixes it. Before a show, the class looks at the art together and fixes what is wrong. Not because it is bad. So everyone can enjoy it. A sculpture near the edge might fall: move it to the middle. A collage curling up needs pressing flat. A print with a smudge can be printed again. Children want to throw work away. Fix ONE thing, together. Tap a change and see what it does.

My journal, the whole year This is everything you made in every lesson this year. Which came first? What would you change now? This is everything you made in every lesson this year. Which came first? Then pick one, and say what you would change now. Children think their first work was bad because it was first. It was not bad. It was where you started. Tap the thing you made first.
